edit_from_base: 'an AnimationTree with a state machine' -> 'keyframes on an AnimationPlayer'
prompt: Animate the player (idle, run, jump, fall) using keyframes on an AnimationPlayer.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Review player.gd and the Player scene to see how movement states (on floor, moving horizontally, rising, falling) are currently determined, and check the Sprite2D's spritesheet or frame setup (hframes/vframes or separate textures). This tells me which frames exist for idle, run, jump, and fall.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of the Player scene, and set its root node so track paths resolve to the Sprite2D correctly.
3. Create four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall, setting appropriate lengths and loop modes (looping for idle and run, non-looping or holding the last frame for jump and fall).
4. For each animation, add a property track on the Sprite2D's frame (or texture) property and insert keyframes at the right times, using discrete/nearest update mode so frames snap rather than interpolate.
5. Optionally add keyframes for small extras like sprite offset or scale squash/stretch on jump and fall, and set the idle animation as autoplay.
6. Update player.gd to choose which animation to play each physics frame based on velocity and floor state (idle when still on floor, run when moving on floor, jump when moving upward, fall when moving downward), only calling play when the animation changes. Also handle sprite flipping based on horizontal direction.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test each transition (standing, running, jumping, walking off a ledge, landing), adjusting keyframe timing, loop settings, and the animation-selection logic for glitches like flickering or stuck animations.
8. Verify the enemy scenes and TileMapLayer are unaffected and that the Player scene saves cleanly, then save the scene.

1. Inspect the Player scene and player.gd to learn the sprite sheet layout (Sprite2D hframes/vframes or frame regions) and which movement states already exist (on floor, moving, rising, falling).
2. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of Player and create four animations: idle, run, jump, fall, setting a sensible length for each and enabling looping on idle and run only.
3. Add keyframe tracks to each animation for the Sprite2D frame property, inserting keys at the correct times for each pose (for example a 2-4 frame breathing loop for idle, 6-8 frames for run, single or short sequences for jump and fall).
4. Tune timing and interpolation so frame tracks use discrete/nearest updates, set run to a comfortable playback speed, and optionally key small offsets or scale on the sprite for squash and stretch.
5. Update player.gd to choose the animation each physics frame: fall when airborne and moving down, jump when airborne and moving up, run when on the floor with horizontal input, otherwise idle.
6. Flip the sprite horizontally based on the last horizontal direction, and avoid restarting an animation that is already playing.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test walking, jumping off platforms, falling from ledges, and landing to confirm transitions look right and nothing flickers.
8. Adjust frame timings or transition conditions based on what is seen in play, and save the Player scene.

1. Inspect the Player scene and the Sprite2D's texture to confirm whether it is a sprite sheet, and note its frame size, frame counts per action, and the Sprite2D's hframes/vframes settings. Also read player.gd to see how it tracks velocity, floor contact, and facing direction.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer as a child of the Player node and create four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall, each with a sensible length and loop mode (looping for idle and run, non-looping or holding the last frame for jump and fall).
3. For each animation, add a track on the Sprite2D's frame property and insert keyframes at the right times so the correct frames display, using discrete (non-interpolated) update mode so frames snap rather than blend.
4. Tune each animation's length and step spacing to give a natural frame rate, for example a slower idle cycle, a faster run cycle, and a single or short-hold pose for jump and fall.
5. If the sprite sheet has different art per action, either use separate textures with a texture track keyed alongside the frame track or consolidate them into one sheet so a single frame track works.
6. In player.gd, add a small animation-selection step that runs each physics frame and picks idle, run, jump, or fall from floor contact, horizontal speed, and vertical velocity sign, only calling play when the chosen animation changes.
7. Flip the sprite horizontally based on movement direction so the run animation faces the correct way, and set the default animation to idle so the player starts in a valid state.
8. Run level_01.tscn to verify each state transitions correctly (standing, running, jumping, falling, landing), fix any timing or flicker issues, and confirm that both enemy scenes and the TileMapLayer are unaffected.

1. Inspect the Player scene, its Sprite2D texture, and player.gd to learn how the sprite sheet is sliced (hframes/vframes or separate textures) and how movement, jump, and fall states are currently determined.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of Player, and confirm the Sprite2D frame, flip, and texture properties are the ones that will be keyed.
3. Create the four animations (idle, run, jump, fall) in the AnimationPlayer, setting sensible lengths and loop modes: looping for idle and run, non-looping or clamped for jump and fall.
4. For each animation, add a track on the Sprite2D frame property (or texture, if using separate images) and insert keyframes at the right times, using discrete/nearest update mode so frames snap rather than blend.
5. Set idle as the autoplay animation and tune keyframe timing so run cycles at a speed that matches the player's movement speed.
6. In player.gd, add a small state-selection step in the physics loop that picks idle, run, jump, or fall from floor contact, horizontal velocity, and vertical velocity sign, and only calls play when the animation actually changes.
7. Handle horizontal facing by flipping the Sprite2D based on input direction rather than keying separate left and right animations.
8. Run level_01.tscn and test each state (standing, running, jumping, falling off a ledge, landing), then adjust keyframes, loop settings, and transitions until they look correct.

1. Review player.gd and the Player node to see how movement states are currently determined (velocity, is_on_floor) and check the Sprite2D's spritesheet layout (frame count, hframes/vframes) so the animations can map to real frames.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer as a child of the Player node, and create four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall, setting idle and run to loop and jump and fall to play once or hold their last frame.
3. For each animation, add keyframe tracks on the Sprite2D's frame (or texture region) property, timing the keys to suit the animation length and the desired frames per second.
4. Where the art calls for it, add extra tracks such as flip or offset adjustments, and use the AnimationPlayer's default blend time so transitions between states look smooth.
5. Edit player.gd so that each physics frame it picks the correct animation from state: on floor and still gives idle, on floor and moving gives run, airborne with upward velocity gives jump, and airborne with downward velocity gives fall.
6. Make the script flip the Sprite2D horizontally based on movement direction, and only call play when the chosen animation actually changes so animations are not restarted every frame.
7. Run level_01.tscn and exercise running, jumping, falling off ledges, and landing on platforms, checking that every transition triggers the right animation and the loops look clean.
8. Tune frame timing, loop modes, and blend settings based on playtesting, and confirm the enemy scenes and level are unaffected by the changes.

1. Check the Player's Sprite2D for its spritesheet and set its frame layout (hframes/vframes or region) so each idle, run, jump, and fall frame can be addressed by index. Note which frames belong to each action.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of the Player scene, with its root pointed at the Player so tracks can reach the Sprite2D.
3. Create four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall, setting sensible lengths, with looping on for idle and run and off for jump and fall.
4. In each animation, add a property track on the Sprite2D frame and insert keyframes at even time intervals, using discrete (non-interpolated) update mode so frames snap rather than blend.
5. Tune per-animation timing, for example a slower idle cycle, a faster run cycle, and short one-shot jump and fall sequences, and set idle as the autoplay default.
6. In player.gd, get a reference to the AnimationPlayer and add logic that picks the animation each physics frame: fall when airborne and moving down, jump when airborne and moving up, run when grounded with horizontal input, otherwise idle.
7. Flip the sprite horizontally based on movement direction and only request a new animation when the state changes, so animations are not restarted every frame.
8. Run level_01.tscn and verify each state in play, including walking off a ledge, jumping, landing, and turning around, then adjust keyframe timing and transitions as needed.

1. Check the Player scene's Sprite2D to learn how the sprite art is set up (single frames, a sprite sheet, or atlas) and how player.gd currently moves the character and reads input. This tells me which animation properties to key and what states the script can expose.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of the Player and, if the sprite is a sheet, set the Sprite2D's horizontal and vertical frame counts so individual frames can be keyed by index. Confirm the AnimationPlayer's root node points at the Player.
3. Create four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall, setting a sensible length and loop mode for each (idle and run loop, jump and fall do not or hold the last frame). Set the step and frame rate so keyframes snap to clean intervals.
4. For each animation, add a track on the Sprite2D frame property (or its texture region) and insert keyframes in order, using the idle frames for a slow breathing cycle and the run frames at a faster cadence. For jump and fall, key the single rise and descent poses, adding a small scale or offset track if a squash or stretch feel is wanted.
5. Add a flip handling approach, either keying nothing and flipping the Sprite2D from the script based on horizontal direction, or adding a flip track only if the art is directional. Keep the collision shape untouched so animation never changes physics.
6. Edit player.gd to choose the animation each physics frame from the character's state: on the floor with near-zero horizontal speed plays idle, on the floor with movement plays run, airborne with upward velocity plays jump, and airborne with downward velocity plays fall. Only call play when the target animation differs from the current one so loops are not restarted.
7. Set idle as the autoplay or default animation and, if transitions look abrupt, set small blend times between animations in the AnimationPlayer.
8. Run level_01.tscn and test standing, running in both directions, jumping, walking off a ledge, and landing, adjusting keyframe timing and loop settings until the transitions look right. Verify the enemies and TileMapLayer are unaffected.

1. Prepare the sprite art: confirm the Player's Sprite2D texture is a sprite sheet (or set of frames) covering idle, run, jump, and fall, and set Hframes/Vframes (or region) so each frame can be selected by index.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of the Player scene and create a new animation library with four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall.
3. For each animation, set the length and loop mode (loop on for idle and run, off or hold-last-frame for jump and fall) and choose a sensible step/snap so frames land on clean intervals.
4. Add a property track for the Sprite2D frame to each animation and insert keyframes at the right timestamps (e.g. several for idle and run, one or two for jump and fall), using the frame index with discrete update mode.
5. Optionally add keyframes for Sprite2D flip or offset, or for the CollisionShape2D, only if the poses need different hitbox or alignment values, keeping the collision shape stable otherwise.
6. In player.gd, get a reference to the AnimationPlayer and add logic in the physics process that picks the animation from state: on floor and still is idle, on floor and moving is run, airborne with upward velocity is jump, airborne with downward velocity is fall.
7. Flip the sprite horizontally based on movement direction, and only call play when the chosen animation differs from the current one so animations are not restarted every frame.
8. Run level_01.tscn and test each transition (idle to run, jumping, falling off platforms, landing), then tune keyframe timing, loop settings, and the velocity thresholds until the motion looks right.

1. Prepare the sprite art: confirm the Player's Sprite2D texture is a sprite sheet and set its frame grid (horizontal and vertical frame counts) so each idle, run, jump, and fall pose maps to a known frame index.
2. Add an AnimationPlayer as a child of the Player node, and set its root node to the Player so tracks can target the Sprite2D and other children.
3. Create four animations named idle, run, jump, and fall, setting a sensible length and loop mode for each (loop idle and run; do not loop jump and fall).
4. For each animation, add a property track on the Sprite2D frame and insert keyframes at the right timestamps, using discrete update mode so frames snap rather than blend.
